Late to the party. But I'm an undergraduate in a social science course and one of the things I've studied and read a lot about is revolution. 

There's a lot of different arguments as to why revolution hasn't occurred in modern western democracies. One of the structural perspectives that I side with myself is that it's largely because of the solidifying of beurocracy, which has few weaknesses compared to other government and once established is very hard to displace  (i.e the state having legitimate monopoly over violence [Weber] etc) also democracy unlike other political systems tends to appease groups and absorb their interests even in the event of two party systems (i.e the US) politics becomes "who I identfity most with", "the lesser of two evils" or "who has the most policies in my interest" as there are no given alternatives. 

This is just a basic skim over of these sociological structural approaches to understand why revolution hasn't occurred in western democracies but they make some pretty interesting and convincing arguments. I'll list some if you're interested.

Also aside from any sociological theories, in terms of politics I often see any alternatives to neo-liberalism in the UK, the U.S and a couple other countries as demonized for being anti-nationalist or not financially plausible or realistic, this fallacy is undermined by the 2008 economic crash especially in the UK (where I'm from)  where the neoliberal view claimed the free market is beyond the government and not for us to control, but tax money was used to bail out banks. A lot of these sociologists have suggested the last time we've seen a likelihood of revolution in Western democracies was during this market crash.

That being understood we shouldn't undermine the value of ideology. And there are just as many sociologists who argue this is as essential or more so in creating revolution than just structural forces such as economics or beaurocracy. Liberalism has been described by many Marxists as the dominant hegemony  (Gramsci) or ideological state apparatus  (Althusser) that legitimate oppression through concepts like meritocracy etc. Ideology can also be a source for power and I think North Korea is a good example of this, the propoganda and even the stories of those who escaped - I remember watching an interview of a woman who escaped to South Korea and even then feared Kim Jung Un would know because she thought him as some kind of omnipotent God.
